models.best: Inferred from its principle that gifts create duties to give and return, so neighbours share the work of vaccination drives and sanitation, and care is repaid with help and trust rather than with fees. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that gifts create debts, so health help flows first to kin and allies who can return a favour, while strangers and those who refuse to give back wait for vaccination and clean water and may be cut off from the exchanges that bring them care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Sahlins, Stone Age Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a family farm plans its work around household needs, so sanitation and vaccination are timed to slack seasons and kept within reach of the village, paid for in labour rather than cash. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves consumption, so a household short of labour skips well repairs, latrine work and vaccination trips until the season eases, and households with the fewest workers carry the most risk of disease. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central authority gathers goods into stores and releases them, so one authority can pay for clean water, latrines and medical stores for many districts at once, and keep a reserve for outbreaks. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre allocates what it collects by rank, so vaccines, medical stores and sanitation works reach officials and favoured districts first, while outlying districts wait for what is left in the store. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation

models.best: Inferred from its principle that owners hold labour as property, so they have a stake in keeping the workforce fit, and some owners pay for physicians and medicines for the workforce whose output they sell through trade. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through ownership of people, so the enslaved are denied any schooling, medical care or say over their own health, and sickness among them is counted as a loss of property rather than a public duty. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a lord gives protection and justice in return for service, so the manor keeps its own wells, drains and ponds in working order as part of the lord's duty to the village. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that services are owed to a lord, so drainage, water and vaccination work is demanded on the lord's terms, and tenants tied to the manor cannot leave to seek care elsewhere, so illness is borne where they are held. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that statutes fix training and quality, so the people who vaccinate, clean and treat are trained and tested under the rules of their trade, and masters inspect the work. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that masters control entry and set prices, so access to trained health workers is closed to outsiders, the price of treatment is fixed by the trade, and districts without a licensed member of the trade go unserved. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state seeks a trade surplus, so it pays for sanitation and vaccination of workers, seamen and soldiers who produce and move goods for export and for the colonies. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates production toward national gain, so health spending is steered to export trades and colonial trade, while the wider population is left to pay for its own care and clean water. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Heckscher, Mercantilism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a single tax on land rent funds the state, so drains, water works and vaccination can be paid for from land without taxing labour or trade, and free trade in grain lets food move to districts that are short. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture makes a net product, so public-health budgets are limited to what a land tax yields, city sanitation and the care of workers in trades are treated as unproductive and left unfunded, and when rents fall, health spending falls with them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competing firms and secure property supply what people will pay for, so drains, clean water, screening and medicines are provided by many firms, each answerable to contract. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state protects property and contracts and otherwise stays out, so drainage and clean water are left to landowners and to those who can pay, the poor renting in crowded houses have no claim to sanitation or vaccination, and disease spreads from their homes to the rest of the town. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge of where care, water and screening are wanted, so local providers respond to demand, and fees show where health services are most needed. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that no planner can gather the knowledge spread across many people, so a central vaccination or sanitation plan misjudges where disease and waste lie, and credit-fuelled spending on hospitals builds capacity that later stands idle. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that privatised providers, open trade in medicines and deregulated entry let rival firms compete for vaccines, screening and sanitation contracts, which is meant to keep costs and waiting times down. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state shrinks and controls are cut, so screening and sanitation budgets are the first to fall in a slump, and a private provider may leave thin rural areas unserved once a contract stops paying. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Harvey, A Brief History of Neoliberalism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public spending rises in slumps and falls in booms, so public-health work and the staff who run it keep their jobs in bad times, funded by taxes that rise as the economy recovers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that spending swings with the economy, so a vaccination or screening campaign that needs steady funding for years is stopped in a boom and restarted in a slump, losing trained staff and cold-chain stock each time. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Keynes, The General Theory

models.best: The case The Salk polio vaccine trial and its announcement, 1954 to 1955 records five firms cleared to make the vaccine on the same day, so several makers were authorised at once rather than one. Its figures are unconfirmed: most sources are anniversary pieces and blogs, and a 113-page evaluation report exists and was not read, so the figures should be checked against it.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that competitive markets need a legal order that curbs monopoly, so without enforced rules one large producer or insurer can dominate vaccines, screening or sanitation and set its own terms, and social insurance may leave people outside the largest schemes without cover. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft

models.best: Inferred from its principle that universal public services are paid for by high taxes, so vaccination, screening and clean water reach every household free at the point of use, and national wage bargaining keeps health-sector pay on one scale. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a single public system funded by high taxes sets one schedule for vaccination and screening for everyone, so local needs can go unmet, and if the tax base shrinks, cover shrinks for every household at once. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs credit and targets to chosen industries and disciplines firms by performance, so medicines, vaccines and water equipment can be made at home, and firms that miss their targets lose support. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state picks favoured industries, so public-health supplies are steered toward chosen producers, screening and sanitation are sidelined when they do not serve export targets, and firms that miss targets lose support even where patients still depend on them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Amsden, Asia's Next Giant

models.best: Inferred from its principle that land values are created by the community around them, so drains, water and clinics paid for from public funds raise land values, and a tax on land returns that gain to the public that paid for them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a land tax falls on landowners, so a fall in land values or rents in a slump leaves water, drainage and clinics short of funds, and landowners who see rates rise may resist the works that pay for care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that planned associations built by example can share a clinic, clean water and a sanitation scheme among members, so care is organised by the community that uses it and not by a distant wage market. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a community built by example depends on the goodwill of its founders, so when the founders leave or the example is not copied, clinics, water and sanitation schemes lapse, and outsiders have no public duty to step in. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit is lent at cost and rent on property is abolished, so workers' mutual funds pay for clean water, drains and vaccines in their own districts, and no landlord collects rent from the works. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free contracts are made between equals, so a small mutual society may lack the funds or staff for screening and outbreak control, and a bad year with no lender at cost leaves health services without reserves. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and vote on the firms they use, so patients, staff and local people set the priorities for screening, vaccination and sanitation together, and any surplus is shared between users and workers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that each member has one vote, so a local majority can vote to cut screening or sanitation for an unpopular minority of users, and a small cooperative may not pool enough reserves to meet an outbreak. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods are shared by need within communes, so vaccines, screening and clean water go to whoever needs them without a means test, and neighbours organise campaigns by free association. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no state and no contract, so no body is bound to keep a sanitation or vaccination scheme running, and in a crisis the resources and volunteers of a commune may be stretched beyond what it can cover, with no outside duty to help. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' organisations run industry directly, so health and sanitation staff in the unions set standards for vaccination, screening and cleaning in their own sectors, and strikes can press for safe working conditions. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that unions run industry through strikes, so a stoppage can halt water, sewerage and clinic services for the public, and the demands of workers may be met before the needs of patients. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail

models.best: The case Chadwick's sanitary inquiry and the Public Health Act of 1848 shows a central Board of Health created by the Act, with localities urged to appoint boards and medical officers and to link homes to clean water supplies and sewerage, though no measured outcome is given. Sources differ on when Chadwick's Board of Health role ended, so no end date is given.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that public enterprise is run by municipal and national officials through gradual reform, so drains, water and clinics reach poor districts slowly, and a national minimum set from the centre may stay low for districts with the worst disease rates. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the Fabian Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control through councils, so nurses, technicians and patients sit on the councils that run clinics, water works and sanitation, with the state as one partner among several. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that several partners share control, so responsibility for vaccination or sanitation is split among councils and the state, and when the partners disagree a campaign may stall while no single body answers for an outbreak. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry

models.best: The case The Soviet sanitary-epidemiological service shows a centralised network built before the Second World War, which a paper hosted by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention describes as a network for surveillance and control of preventable disease, with a central planning role. One source gives a different year for the founding decree, which looks like a typo, so no year is given here.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that central plans set output and investment, so vaccination and sanitation targets may be met on paper while local needs go unmet, and health posts may be drawn into industrial drives when the plan requires labour. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System

models.best: Inferred from its principle that managers follow market prices within public ownership, so clinics and water utilities respond to what districts will pay for, while a central board sets the rules and the investment for all. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules and the investment, so managers who follow prices may cut screening or sanitation in poor districts where it does not pay, and the board may be slow to correct the gap. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Yugoslav workers' self-management

models.best: Inferred from its principle that distribution follows need, so vaccination, screening and clean water are given to each person by need rather than by ability to pay, and public health becomes a common duty once classes have gone. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state withers away only after classes disappear, so while a state still exists, it decides what need is for everyone, and patients may have little way to contest its judgement about treatment, screening or sanitation. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme

models.best: Inferred from its principle that key sectors stay public while markets are allowed, so the state keeps hospitals and vaccine supply in public hands, private clinics and suppliers compete at the edges, and reform is tried first in special zones. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that reform is gradual and zone-based under party direction, so care and sanitation outside the zones lag behind, and price reform can leave poorer patients paying more while the rules are still being set. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Naughton, The Chinese Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that councils of workers and consumers propose and revise plans in rounds, so screening, vaccination and sanitation budgets are set by the people who deliver and use them, with neither a market nor a central planner deciding. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that plans are made through repeated rounds of proposals, so an outbreak that needs a fast decision may wait for the next round, and balancing jobs in complexity may leave skilled screening and sanitation posts under-filled. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into corporations, so health and sanitation work is planned in the same bodies as employers and unions, and medical and industrial resources are coordinated toward national goals. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state directs industry toward national goals, including war, so vaccines, sanitation works and medical supplies may be turned to military needs first, and the corporations may be used to hold workers and patients to the state's priorities. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Nazi Four-Year Plan

models.best: Inferred from its principle that zakat redistributes wealth to the poor, so clinics, clean water and vaccination for poor households can be funded by alms, while finance shares profit and risk, so health projects are funded by shared risk rather than by debt. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that zakat and trust carry the cost of care, so when alms and trust fall short, health projects that cannot share profit may go unfunded, and patients outside a trusted network may have no route to credit for treatment. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System

models.best: Inferred from its principle that production is small-scale, local and non-violent, so clinics, water and sanitation are kept close to the people they serve, and care is judged by well-being rather than by volume. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that consumption is kept moderate, so costly screening, new treatments and expensive vaccines may be judged excess, and small local providers may lack the scale to run outbreak response or a national vaccination programme. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful

models.best: Inferred from its principle that decisions stay with the smallest competent body, so families, parishes and local clinics decide on vaccination, sanitation and screening, and a just wage keeps the staff who provide care in work. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that small property owners and small firms carry the costs of their own care, so a household or small firm unable to pay for drains, water or screening goes without, and a national scheme may be judged too large for the smallest competent body to run. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Belloc, The Servile State

models.best: Inferred from its principle that everyone has a social floor and activity stays within planetary limits, so clean water, sanitation, vaccination and basic screening reach all people without relying on growth in output to pay for them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no growth imperative, so public-health budgets may be held flat while populations grow or new disease risks appear, and the social floor may be set low enough to keep activity within limits, leaving some people without screening or treatment. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Raworth, Doughnut Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, so people can pay for their own screening, clean water and sanitation, and no one is kept from basic care for lack of cash. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that income is unconditional, so the state does not directly fund sanitation, vaccination or clinics, and people who spend the income elsewhere may still lack clean water or care, while the revenue from land and natural resources may not match what public health needs. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government which issues its own currency can fund vaccination, screening and sanitation without debt as the limit, so public-health spending can be sized to need, with inflation as the check. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, so public-health spending may grow until prices rise sharply, and higher prices can make medicines, staff and water works costly to buy, leaving the poorest with the least care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth

models.best: The case Worldwide eradication of smallpox shows a mandate from the World Health Assembly in 1966 and validation of the outcome by a body of experts from 19 countries in Geneva in December 1979. Vaccines alone did not produce the result, which relied on decades of work, diplomacy and technical innovation.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that users monitor and enforce their own rules, so when a community does not monitor vaccination coverage or enforce sanitation rules, free-riders leave gaps that let disease return to all, and rules made locally may not connect to the wider bodies that control outbreaks. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons

compromise.summary: A mixed public system sets national standards for vaccination, screening and sanitation, financed from general taxation. Local boards and several licensed suppliers deliver the work under rules agreed by the bodies that share the goal, checked each year by an independent expert panel.
compromise.details: Keeps: shared rules checked by an expert panel (Commons governance; Worldwide eradication of smallpox); local delivery under a national standard (Fabian socialism; Chadwick's sanitary inquiry and the Public Health Act of 1848); several licensed suppliers, figures unconfirmed (Social market economy; The Salk polio vaccine trial and its announcement, 1954 to 1955); tax-funded care, free at the point of use (Nordic social democracy). Blocks: favours by kin or rank, guarded by a statutory entitlement; campaigns stopped in each boom or slump, guarded by ring-fenced funding; targets met on paper, guarded by independent audits. Test: coverage, notified cases, water and sewerage access and cost per person, measured yearly in every district for ten years. Source: Ohio State University, The WHO and the eradication of smallpox; Victorian Web, Edwin Chadwick and the sanitary report; University of Michigan School of Public Health, 1955 polio vaccine trial announcement; Sahlins, Stone Age Economics; Keynes, The General Theory; Kornai, The Socialist System; Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism.
